About this programme

UCR currently cannot construct a sufficiently close programme for a meaningful curriculum comparison.

Religious Studies at the University of Amsterdam studies religious diversity, traditions, texts and practices through historical, literary and social-scientific approaches. The programme gives particular attention to contemporary religion and spirituality, Western esotericism and research in Amsterdam. This example includes the first-year Arabic package.

UCR offers substantial related study in comparative myth, religious art and material culture, ancient ritual, philosophy, social inquiry and religious freedom. These connections do not develop into sustained study of religious traditions, sacred interpretation or contemporary religious practice across a full programme. The wider course combinations shift towards general cultural, philosophical or social study.

Arts and Culture Studies at Erasmus University Rotterdam examines how arts and creative industries work in society. It combines cultural sociology, economics, management, media and heritage with research methods. Students develop a focus area, complete an arts-and-culture internship and undertake an individual graduation project.

The three UCR programmes offer different combinations of relevant fields. Matches show important shared content rather than course equivalence; blank cells preserve substantive differences. None of these programmes is an arts-and-health pathway. UCR’s general sociology and organisational study do not reproduce IBACS’s specialist cultural-sector curriculum or mandatory placement.

Some required study is unverified and excluded.

What this comparison shows

A qualified academic comparison of the documented scope of International Bachelor Arts and Culture Studies at Erasmus University Rotterdam with 3 illustrative UCR study compositions.

CLOSEST UCR MATCH
Arts, culture, economy & society

Art history, heritage and literature connect with media, sociology, economics and organisations. Research methods support the study of cultural works, markets and social contexts; these general disciplines complement the arts without reproducing IBACS’s specialist cultural-sector sequence.

ADDITIONAL UCR OPTION
Culture, society & public life

Art, heritage and history connect with sociology, law, philosophy and public policy to explore inequality, collective life and social conflict. Qualitative and quantitative methods support inquiry into culture’s place in public life; this is not an arts-and-health pathway.

ADDITIONAL UCR OPTION
Culture, media & digital society

Film, media and literature connect with rhetoric, communication, audience research and digital change. Sociology and data methods support the study of representation, platforms and cultural participation; the programme does not provide a specialist cultural-sociology sequence.

Biology across organisms, ecosystems & health

Study living systems from biodiversity, evolution and ecosystems to cells, biochemistry, human physiology, genetics and disease. Laboratory work, statistics and data analysis support these biological questions; environmental science, sustainability governance and ethics add complementary perspectives.

ADDITIONAL UCR OPTION
Ecology, climate & environmental biology

Study biodiversity, evolution, ecosystems and conservation alongside climate change and environmental systems. Spatial analysis, soils, biogeochemistry and sustainability research connect ecological questions with environmental assessment; governance, justice and resource geoscience provide complementary approaches.

ADDITIONAL UCR OPTION
Human biology, neuroscience & health psychology

Study molecular and cellular biology, human physiology, infection, genetics and disease together with neurobiology and cognition. A substantial psychology strand examines behaviour, mental health, development and assessment. Laboratory work, epidemiology, statistics and research synthesis support this combination; it is not a specialist medical or clinical qualification. Normative ethical reasoning complements the biological and psychological inquiry; this is not professional clinical-psychology training.
